# Investigative Report: Linking the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge Thefts to Lazarus Group

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports a strong public attribution of both the March 2022 Ronin Bridge theft and the June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge theft to North Korea-linked Lazarus Group. The link is based on three mutually reinforcing categories of evidence:

1. **Public attribution:** Elliptic reported that the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) identified the Ronin exploiter’s Ethereum address as belonging to Lazarus Group. Elliptic later reported that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group was responsible for the Harmony Horizon Bridge theft.
2. **Shared laundering patterns:** Both thefts involved the movement of stolen assets through decentralized exchanges, Tornado Cash, intermediary wallets, and later privacy-enhancing or cross-chain DeFi services. Elliptic specifically stated that the Harmony laundering pattern mirrored the pattern previously observed in the Ronin theft.
3. **Wallet and transaction evidence:** The sources describe identifiable chains of transactions from the stolen assets into intermediary wallets, mixers, DeFi protocols, and cryptocurrency exchanges. In the Ronin case, Elliptic reported that it labeled addresses associated with the exploiter, while Chainalysis described tracing activity across more than 12,000 addresses and following funds to cash-out points.

The evidence does **not**, however, independently establish a separate APT38 attribution. The supplied sources identify the actor as Lazarus Group and, in the Chainalysis material, refer more generally to North Korea-linked groups. No source provided here explicitly states that APT38 conducted either theft. Accordingly, the most defensible conclusion is that the two incidents are publicly attributed to Lazarus Group, while a specific Lazarus Group–APT38 equivalence remains unsupported by the supplied evidence.

## Scope and source assessment

This assessment uses the four distinct source URLs supplied in the case materials. Two URLs are repeated in the input and are treated as single sources rather than duplicated evidence.

| Source ID | Publisher and date | Main evidentiary contribution | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Elliptic, May 9, 2023 | Reports FBI confirmation of Lazarus Group attribution for Harmony; describes Tornado Cash and Railgun laundering | Most recent and directly relevant source for Harmony attribution |
| S2 | Chainalysis, September 8, 2022 | Describes Ronin theft, laundering stages, chain-hopping, address scale, and seizures | Directly relevant forensic and recovery account for Ronin |
| S3 | Elliptic, March 29, 2022, updated April 14, 2022 | Reports Ronin theft details, OFAC identification of Lazarus Group, and early laundering movements | Direct attribution and contemporaneous transaction account |
| S4 | Elliptic, undated resource page | General Elliptic research index; no additional case-specific evidence in the supplied extract | Limited relevance; not relied upon for substantive conclusions |

The primary evidentiary weight is therefore assigned to S1, S2, and S3. S4 is included in the references because it was supplied, but the extracted content does not provide additional facts about either theft.

## Incident profiles

### Ronin Bridge theft

The Ronin Network announced on March 29, 2022, that 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC had been stolen from its cross-chain bridge. Elliptic valued the stolen assets at approximately $540 million at the time of the theft and described the incident as the second-largest crypto theft at that point. The theft occurred six days before public disclosure. The affected network later stated that the incident was discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt failed. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

According to the Ronin postmortem as summarized by Elliptic, the attacker obtained the private cryptographic keys of five of the bridge’s nine validators. That threshold was sufficient to approve withdrawals from the bridge. Elliptic reported that the evidence pointed toward a socially engineered attack rather than a technical flaw. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Chainalysis provided a substantially similar account, stating that Lazarus Group gained access to five of nine validator keys and used that majority to approve withdrawals of 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC. Chainalysis stated that the theft exceeded $600 million in its presentation of the incident, reflecting a different valuation point from Elliptic’s approximately $540 million valuation at the time of theft. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

### Harmony Horizon Bridge theft

The Harmony Horizon Bridge was exploited on June 24, 2022, for approximately $99.7 million. Elliptic described the bridge as servicing the Harmony blockchain and noted prior concerns about its centralization and vulnerability to social-engineering attacks. The source compared the incident with the earlier Ronin theft, which had also involved a cross-chain bridge and had been attributed to Lazarus Group. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Elliptic stated that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group was behind the Harmony theft. The same source characterized the announcement as confirming Elliptic’s earlier attribution, which had been based on similarities between the laundering behavior observed after the Harmony theft and the group’s prior blockchain laundering patterns. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

## Public attribution evidence

### Ronin attribution

The Ronin attribution has two distinct public elements in the supplied sources.

First, Elliptic reported that on April 14, 2022, OFAC sanctioned the Ethereum address associated with the Ronin Bridge exploiter and identified its owner as Lazarus Group, described as a North Korean state hacking group. The stated sanctions purpose was to prevent the group from cashing out remaining funds through U.S.-based exchanges. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Second, Chainalysis described its own investigation as involving North Korean-linked hackers and stated that the funds were stolen by actors affiliated with Lazarus Group. Chainalysis also reported that its investigation contributed to the seizure of more than $30 million in cryptocurrency, representing approximately 10% of the total stolen funds when accounting for changes in asset prices between theft and seizure. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

The OFAC identification, as reported by Elliptic, is the strongest attribution evidence in the provided materials because it connects a specifically identified Ethereum address to Lazarus Group through a government sanctions action. The Chainalysis account independently reinforces the North Korea/Lazarus attribution but does not provide wallet addresses in the supplied text.

### Harmony attribution

The Harmony attribution is presented most directly in Elliptic’s May 2023 report. Elliptic stated that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group as the actor behind the June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge hack. The report also stated that Elliptic had previously identified the connection based on similarities in blockchain laundering behavior. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

This source is later than the Ronin reporting and specifically describes a subsequent FBI confirmation. On the evidence supplied, the Harmony attribution is therefore a public law-enforcement-confirmed attribution as reported by Elliptic, supplemented by Elliptic’s transaction-pattern analysis.

## Laundering-pattern linkage

### Shared use of Tornado Cash

The strongest operational link between the two cases is the reported reuse of Tornado Cash-related laundering behavior.

For Ronin, Elliptic reported that the attacker first swapped stolen USDC for ETH through decentralized exchanges. The stated rationale was that stablecoins can sometimes be frozen by issuers, whereas converting the assets through DEXs avoided centralized exchange AML and KYC controls. The attacker then moved funds through centralized exchanges, but shifted toward Tornado Cash after those exchanges announced cooperation with law enforcement. Elliptic reported that approximately $80.3 million in ETH had been sent through Tornado Cash by April 14, 2022, with another approximately $9.7 million held in intermediary wallets and apparently prepared for laundering. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Chainalysis described a broader five-stage pattern associated with North Korea-linked DeFi laundering:

1. Stolen ETH sent to intermediary wallets.
2. ETH mixed in batches through Tornado Cash.
3. ETH swapped for bitcoin.
4. Bitcoin mixed in batches.
5. Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cash-out.

Chainalysis stated that Lazarus Group replicated this process with substantial portions of the Ronin proceeds. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

For Harmony, Elliptic reported that the funds were programmatically structured through Tornado Cash. Elliptic researchers stated that the laundering methods mirrored those used by Lazarus Group in the Ronin Bridge theft. Elliptic estimated that more than $555 million connected to the two hacks had been sent through Tornado Cash: more than $468 million from Ronin and approximately $96 million from Harmony. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The numerical comparison is significant. The reported $96 million attributed to Harmony through Tornado Cash is broadly consistent with the approximately $99.7 million stolen from Horizon, subject to transaction fees, asset movements, valuation differences, and the source’s rounding. The reported more than $468 million from Ronin likewise represents a substantial portion of the original theft.

### Post-sanctions movement to Railgun and other DeFi services

Elliptic reported that after Tornado Cash was sanctioned by OFAC in August 2022, funds associated with the Harmony theft remained dormant in several post-mixer addresses until January 2023. In January, the funds began to be structured into deposits into Railgun, a privacy-oriented DeFi protocol that Elliptic described as functioning similarly to a mixer. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Elliptic estimated that around 70% of the Ether sent through Railgun to that date consisted of funds from the Harmony hack. Elliptic’s interpretation was that the high proportion of Harmony-related funds reduced the effectiveness of the obfuscation because the anonymity set was relatively small. This is an assessment by Elliptic, not an independently verified finding in the supplied materials. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Chainalysis separately reported that, after Tornado Cash sanctions, Lazarus Group used DeFi services to chain-hop between blockchains and swap assets. One example described ETH being bridged from Ethereum to BNB Chain, swapped for USDD, and then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Chainalysis stated that hundreds of similar transactions were conducted across several blockchains in connection with the Ronin proceeds. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

The Harmony and Ronin cases therefore exhibit a common adaptive pattern: movement from DEXs and intermediary wallets toward Tornado Cash, followed by use of alternative privacy or cross-chain mechanisms after sanctions and exchange scrutiny increased.

## Wallet evidence and exchange endpoints

### Ronin wallet evidence

Elliptic reported that, by April 14, 2022, approximately $433 million remained in the attacker’s original wallet, while other funds had been moved into intermediary wallets or through Tornado Cash. Elliptic stated that its investigators had labeled the addresses associated with the attacker in its systems so that clients could be alerted if they received funds from them. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Chainalysis stated that the laundering process had involved more than 12,000 cryptocurrency addresses. This figure indicates a large and complex transaction graph, although the supplied source does not list the addresses individually. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

### Harmony wallet and exchange evidence

For Harmony, Elliptic described post-Tornado withdrawals into several addresses where the funds remained dormant until January 2023. The source then identified subsequent deposits into three cryptoasset exchanges. Two of those exchanges, Binance and Huobi, reportedly identified, blocked, and seized part of the funds. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

This evidence is consistent with the proposition that the laundering network was not merely theoretical or limited to mixer deposits. The funds continued to move through identifiable addresses and eventually reached centralized exchange infrastructure, where compliance controls and blockchain analytics enabled intervention. The supplied materials do not provide the exact wallet addresses, transaction hashes, seizure amounts, or dates for the Binance and Huobi actions; those details should not be inferred.

## Relationship to APT38

The case objective refers to “Lazarus Group/APT38,” but the supplied sources do not provide sufficient evidence to make a specific APT38 attribution.

The sources use the following terms:

- **Lazarus Group:** explicitly identified by OFAC, as reported by Elliptic, in relation to the Ronin exploiter’s Ethereum address.
- **Lazarus Group:** explicitly identified by Elliptic as responsible for the Harmony theft based on FBI confirmation.
- **North Korea-linked groups or hackers:** used by Chainalysis in describing the Ronin investigation.
- **APT38:** not named in any of the supplied source extracts.

It is therefore appropriate to treat Lazarus Group as the supported actor label and to leave APT38 as an unconfirmed or unsupported association in this report. A report that equated Lazarus Group and APT38 without additional evidence would exceed the supplied record.

## Comparative findings

| Question | Ronin Bridge | Harmony Horizon Bridge | Linkage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Theft date | Six days before March 29, 2022 public announcement; incident described as occurring March 23, 2022 | June 24, 2022 | Separate incidents, both involving cross-chain bridges ([S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft)) |
| Approximate amount | $540 million at theft valuation; Chainalysis describes more than $600 million | $99.7 million, commonly rounded to $100 million | Both were major bridge thefts |
| Technical/access method | Five of nine validator keys reportedly compromised through social engineering | Bridge centralization and social engineering vulnerability discussed; exact exploit mechanics not supplied | Similar social-engineering context, but not identical proof |
| Attribution | OFAC identified exploiter address as Lazarus Group, as reported by Elliptic | FBI confirmation reported by Elliptic | Strong public attribution to Lazarus Group |
| Laundering | DEX swaps, intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, Bitcoin mixing, chain-hopping, crypto-to-fiat services | Tornado Cash, dormant intermediary addresses, Railgun, exchange deposits | Strongest substantive linkage |
| Wallet evidence | Original wallet, intermediary wallets, more than 12,000 addresses, labeled exploiter addresses | Post-mixer addresses, Railgun deposits, three exchange destinations | Common use of distributed wallet networks |
| Recovery/intervention | More than $30 million seized, according to Chainalysis | Binance and Huobi reportedly blocked and seized part of the funds | Exchange and analytics cooperation in both cases |

## Findings

### Finding 1: Are the Ronin and Harmony thefts publicly attributed to the same actor?

Yes. The Ronin exploiter’s address was publicly associated with Lazarus Group through the OFAC action reported by Elliptic, while Elliptic reported that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group’s responsibility for the Harmony theft. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

### Finding 2: What links the incidents beyond attribution?

The strongest link is the reuse of laundering behavior: DEX conversion, intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, and later alternative DeFi or cross-chain obfuscation. Elliptic expressly said the Harmony laundering pattern mirrored the Ronin pattern. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

### Finding 3: Is there direct wallet evidence in the supplied record?

Yes, but not complete address-level evidence. The sources describe the Ronin exploiter’s original and intermediary wallets, Elliptic-labeled addresses, Tornado Cash flows, and a laundering graph involving more than 12,000 addresses. For Harmony, the sources describe post-mixer withdrawal addresses, Railgun deposits, and deposits into three exchanges. The actual addresses and transaction hashes are not included in the supplied material. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

### Finding 4: Does the evidence establish APT38 involvement?

No. The supplied sources establish Lazarus Group and North Korea-linked attribution but do not name APT38. Any APT38 conclusion would require additional evidence not present here.

## Conclusion

The supplied evidence supports the conclusion that the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge thefts were separate operations publicly attributed to the same North Korea-linked actor, Lazarus Group. The attribution is strongest for Ronin because OFAC, as reported by Elliptic, identified the exploiter’s Ethereum address as Lazarus Group. It is strongest for Harmony because Elliptic reported an FBI confirmation.

The operational linkage is also persuasive. Both cases involved bridge thefts followed by structured laundering through intermediary wallets and privacy-enhancing services. Tornado Cash was central to both laundering narratives, and Elliptic specifically identified the Harmony laundering pattern as mirroring the Ronin pattern. Subsequent adaptation to Railgun in the Harmony case and cross-chain DeFi chain-hopping in the Ronin case indicates a common effort to evade sanctions, exchange screening, and asset tracing.

My concrete assessment is therefore: **the Ronin and Harmony thefts should be treated as Lazarus Group-linked incidents with high confidence on the basis of public attribution and repeated laundering typologies. The supplied evidence does not justify a separate or equivalent APT38 attribution.**

Similar issues resulted in the criminal organization stealing over $540 million from another cross-chain bridge called Ronin earlier in March 2022. After stealing the funds from Horizon, the Lazarus Group then programmatically structured transactions through Tornado Cash, which is a decentralized Ethereum-based mixer. Elliptic researchers identified that the laundering methods employed mirrored those the Lazarus Group had used when attempting to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge hack, which had also been sent through Tornado Cash. US sanctions US sanctions Tornado Cash was subsequently sanctioned by the US Treasury in August 2022, with Secretary of State Anthony Blinken citing its prolific use by the Lazarus Group to launder funds from its past hacks. This North Korea-linked activity accounts for approximately 5.8% of the nearly $9 billion in total funds sent through the Tornado Cash mixer to date. Elliptic has traced the stolen funds from the Horizon hack through Tornado Cash. This suggests that since the OFAC sanctions on Tornado Cash, North Korea may be turning to lower obfuscating services as an alternative. However, the fact that funds from the Harmony hack comprised such a substantial volume of the Ether passing through Railgun renders the mixing ineffective. As an analogy, imagine if you threw five pennies into a jar full of 100 pennies, it would be extremely difficult for someone to determine which pennies were yours. However, if you threw 70 pennies into a jar with only 30 other pennies in it, then there would be a higher chance of linking those 70 specific pennies back to you. Mixers work in a similar way: when the anonymity set – or volume of other funds in the mixer is low – it makes the mixer less effective at concealing disproportionately large funds transfers. Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks. Railgun Railgun Elliptic’s research suggests that a significant portion of funds – estimated at around 70% – that has been sent through Railgun to date are funds from the Harmony hack. This suggests that since the OFAC sanctions on Tornado Cash, North Korea may be turning to lower obfuscating services as an alternative. However, the fact that funds from the Harmony hack comprised such a substantial volume of the Ether passing through Railgun renders the mixing ineffective. As an analogy, imagine if you threw five pennies into a jar full of 100 pennies, it would be extremely difficult for someone to determine which pennies were yours. However, if you threw 70 pennies into a jar with only 30 other pennies in it, then there would be a higher chance of linking those 70 specific pennies back to you. Mixers work in a similar way: when the anonymity set – or volume of other funds in the mixer is low – it makes the mixer less effective at concealing disproportionately large funds transfers. On-chain data shows that after sending the funds through Railgun, the Lazarus Group has since deposited funds into three cryptoasset exchanges. Two, namely Binance and Huobi, have announced that they have identified, blocked and seized a portion of the funds. This case demonstrates the importance of cryptoasset exchanges utlizing blockchain analytics solutions to identify transactions involving mixing services abused by sanctioned actors such as North Korea. Elliptic’s Holistic wallet and transaction screening solutions enable our customers to identify and block transactions involving these mixing services, including where there may be sanctions implications - such as links to North Korean perpetrated hacks. Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks.
